title: Who logged in to this Windows computer, and when?
lead: Windows writes an event each time an account logs on, fails to log on or logs off. This workflow shows how to export the event logs from an image, read the logon events, check Remote Desktop activity and list the accounts on the computer.
time: 2 to 3 hours on the practice image
evidence: A disk image of a Windows computer, or exported event log files
answers: Which accounts logged on, and how (at the keyboard, over the network or by Remote Desktop)
When each logon started and ended
Which logons failed, and from which address
Whether someone used Remote Desktop, and from where
Which local accounts exist and when each was last used
need: A forensic image of the Windows computer, or exported .evtx files, or a practice image (see the practice section on this page)
A Windows workstation to run EvtxECmd and Timeline Explorer
The time zone setting of the computer, which you will read in step 2

steps.title: Work on an image, never the original
steps.text: If you start from a real computer, make a forensic image through a write blocker and write down its hash value. Open the image in Autopsy or FTK Imager. If someone gave you only exported log files, hash them on arrival and note who gave them to you and when.

steps.title: Export the log files and registry hives
steps.text: Copy the files below out of the image. In Autopsy, right-click a file and choose Extract File(s). In the log folder, file names show a slash in the log name as %4. Also export the SYSTEM hive: it holds the computer's time zone setting in the TimeZoneInformation key. Event times are stored in UTC, so you need the time zone to explain them in local time.

steps.title: Turn the Security log into a table
steps.text: An .evtx file is a binary format, so you need a parser. EvtxECmd reads it and writes a CSV file with one row per event. Open the CSV in Timeline Explorer, which lets you sort, filter and search large tables. Run the parser again for each log file you exported.

steps.title: Read the successful logons (event 4624)
steps.text: Filter the table for event ID 4624, which means an account was logged on. Look at the account name, the logon type and the source address. Common logon types: 2 is interactive (at the keyboard), 3 is network (for example a shared folder), 5 is a service starting, 7 is an unlock, 10 is Remote Desktop and 11 is a logon with cached credentials. Many 4624 rows are system accounts and services, so filter those out and focus on user accounts.
steps.note: Each logon has a Logon ID. Use it to match a logon to its logoff and to other events of the same session. It is only unique until the computer restarts.

steps.title: Add failures, logoffs and special logons
steps.text: 4625 is a failed logon. Its status codes give the reason, such as a bad password or an unknown user name. 4634 is the end of a session and 4647 is a user asking to log off. 4648 is a logon with explicitly given credentials, which also happens in normal use such as scheduled tasks. 4672 means the new session received sensitive privileges, which is normal for administrators and system accounts. Match them by Logon ID.

steps.title: Check Remote Desktop activity
steps.text: Parse the two Remote Desktop logs the same way. In the LocalSessionManager log, event 21 means a session logon succeeded, 24 means a session was disconnected and 25 means a session was reconnected. In the RemoteConnectionManager log, event 1149 means user authentication succeeded, with the source network address. Authentication is not the same as a full session, so compare with 4624 of logon type 10.

steps.title: Triage fast, then look for gaps
steps.text: Hayabusa and Chainsaw scan a folder of .evtx files with detection rules and point you at unusual events quickly. Treat their output as leads to check in the raw events. Then look for gaps: event 1102 in the Security log means the log was cleared, and the first and last dates in the file show how far back it reaches.
steps.note: A detection rule can flag normal activity. Always open the original event before you write a conclusion.

steps.title: List the accounts in the SAM hive
steps.text: The SAM hive stores the local user accounts. Open it in Registry Explorer under SAM\Domains\Account\Users, or run the SAM plugin of RegRipper. You get the account names, creation dates, last logon times and last password change. Compare the last logon time with the newest 4624 event for the same account.

steps.title: Cross-check and write it down
steps.text: Confirm each important logon from two sources, for example a 4624 event and a LocalSessionManager event, or a last logon time in SAM and the event log. In your notes, record tool names and versions, the source file of each event, the Logon ID and the computer's time zone.

artifacts.name: Security.evtx, event 4624 and 4625
artifacts.tells: Successful and failed logons, with account, logon type and source address

artifacts.name: Security.evtx, events 4634, 4647, 4648, 4672
artifacts.tells: Logoffs, explicit credentials and sessions with sensitive privileges

artifacts.name: TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager log, events 21, 24, 25
artifacts.tells: Remote Desktop and local session logon, disconnect and reconnect

artifacts.name: TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager log, event 1149
artifacts.tells: Successful Remote Desktop authentication, with source address

artifacts.name: Security event 1102
artifacts.tells: The Security log was cleared, and which account did it

artifacts.name: SAM hive
artifacts.tells: Local accounts, creation date, last logon and last password change

artifacts.name: TimeZoneInformation
artifacts.tells: The computer's time zone setting, needed to read times in local time

limits: A logon record shows that an account was used. It does not show which person typed the password or sat at the computer.
The Security log only holds what the audit policy told Windows to record. If logon auditing was off, the events are not there.
Logs roll over. When a log reaches its size limit, old events are overwritten, so a quiet period may only mean the events are gone.
A log can be cleared. Event 1102 shows that it happened, but the cleared events are not recoverable from the log itself.
Event times are stored in UTC, but some tools show local time. Mixing the two is a common mistake, so write down which one you used.
A network address in a logon event can belong to a router, a VPN or a shared computer. It does not identify a person.
Event IDs and fields differ a little between Windows versions. Check the documentation for the version you examine.

practice.name: NIST CFReDS: Data Leakage Case
practice.text: A simulated company data leak on a Windows 7 computer, with a PC image of about 5 GB as a compressed DD file, or about 7.3 GB in E01 format. The case has questions about the user accounts, the last logon and logon and logoff traces. NIST publishes an answer document, so you can check your result.
practice.task: Try question 7 of the case: "Who was the last user to logon into PC?" Use steps 2, 4 and 8, then compare your answer with the published answers.
practice.note: The case does not tell you which events its Security log holds, and some of the logs in steps 6 and 7 may be missing or empty on a Windows 7 computer. If a log is empty, write that down. For more practice with plain .evtx files, the public EVTX-ATTACK-SAMPLES repository on GitHub collects samples of attack techniques. Check its own README before you use it.
